claims.text: The proposed intervention is incorporation of 2–5 wt% silicon during fabrication of a boride-based component.
Adding 2–5 wt% silicon will improve the molten-aluminum corrosion resistance of boride-based components used in hot-dip aluminum plating.
Silicon addition will promote formation of protective silicide phases or a silicide-enriched intermetallic/oxide interface.
The resulting silicide or silicide-enriched interface will act as a diffusion barrier against molten-aluminum attack.
Silicon alloying is expected to alter interfacial phase formation and diffusion behavior.
Alloying-element diffusion during heat treatment can play a critical role in formation of interfacial microstructures.
Silicon-promoted silicide phases or modified oxide layers will reduce the rate of aluminum dissolution.
Silicon addition will minimize selective leaching of the boride.
Selective depletion or dealloying can occur when alloy constituents preferentially react with a molten corrosive medium.

Relative to boride components without silicon, silicon-alloyed components will exhibit lower corrosion current density, reduced mass loss, or slower structural degradation during molten-aluminum exposure.
The beneficial effect is expected only when silicon content is optimized within 2–5 wt%.
Silicon contents above the proposed range could compromise the component microstructure or mechanical properties.
The corrosion benefit will depend on achieving a uniform silicon distribution during fabrication.
The magnitude of the corrosion-resistance improvement may vary with processing conditions and microstructural evolution.
The appropriate experimental baseline is an otherwise identical boride-based component without silicon addition, exposed under identical conditions.
